claim: Nearly 150 million children under-5 years of age were stunted in 2020.
source: Despite recent advances in the prevention and treatment of childhood malnutrition, nearly 150 million children under-5 years of age were stunted in 2020 (UNICEF et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to UNICEF et al., 2021

claim: Stunting is defined as a length- or height-for-age z-score (HAZ) 2 or more standard deviations below the population median.
source: Stunting is defined as a length- or height-for-age z-score (HAZ) 2 or more standard deviations below the population median (de Onis et al., 2013), and is considered both an indicator of underlying deficits (i.e., chronic malnutrition, The World Bank, 2021), as well as a potential contributor to future health problems (e.g., through poor immune system maturation, Rytter et al., 2014; Bourke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Onis et al., 2013

claim: Stunting is considered an indicator of underlying deficits such as chronic malnutrition.
source: Stunting is defined as a length- or height-for-age z-score (HAZ) 2 or more standard deviations below the population median (de Onis et al., 2013), and is considered both an indicator of underlying deficits (i.e., chronic malnutrition, The World Bank, 2021), as well as a potential contributor to future health problems (e.g., through poor immune system maturation, Rytter et al., 2014; Bourke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to The World Bank, 2021

claim: Stunting is a potential contributor to future health problems such as poor immune system maturation.
source: Stunting is defined as a length- or height-for-age z-score (HAZ) 2 or more standard deviations below the population median (de Onis et al., 2013), and is considered both an indicator of underlying deficits (i.e., chronic malnutrition, The World Bank, 2021), as well as a potential contributor to future health problems (e.g., through poor immune system maturation, Rytter et al., 2014; Bourke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rytter et al., 2014 and Bourke et al., 2016

claim: Stunting has been consistently associated with increased risk of morbidity and mortality.
source: Furthermore, stunting has been consistently associated with increased risk of morbidity and mortality, delayed or deficient cognitive development, and reduced educational attainment (McDonald et al., 2013; Black et al., 2013; Olofin et al., 2013; Adair et al., 2013; de Onis and Branca, 2016; Black et al., 2008; Bhaskaram, 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including McDonald et al., 2013; Black et al., 2013; Olofin et al., 2013; Adair et al., 2013; de Onis and Branca, 2016; Black et al., 2008; Bhaskaram, 2002

claim: Stunting has been consistently associated with delayed or deficient cognitive development.
source: Furthermore, stunting has been consistently associated with increased risk of morbidity and mortality, delayed or deficient cognitive development, and reduced educational attainment (McDonald et al., 2013; Black et al., 2013; Olofin et al., 2013; Adair et al., 2013; de Onis and Branca, 2016; Black et al., 2008; Bhaskaram, 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including McDonald et al., 2013; Black et al., 2013; Olofin et al., 2013; Adair et al., 2013; de Onis and Branca, 2016; Black et al., 2008; Bhaskaram, 2002

claim: Stunting has been consistently associated with reduced educational attainment.
source: Furthermore, stunting has been consistently associated with increased risk of morbidity and mortality, delayed or deficient cognitive development, and reduced educational attainment (McDonald et al., 2013; Black et al., 2013; Olofin et al., 2013; Adair et al., 2013; de Onis and Branca, 2016; Black et al., 2008; Bhaskaram, 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including McDonald et al., 2013; Black et al., 2013; Olofin et al., 2013; Adair et al., 2013; de Onis and Branca, 2016; Black et al., 2008; Bhaskaram, 2002

claim: Stunting has been linked with diarrheal diseases across many settings.
source: Stunting has been linked with diarrheal diseases across many settings (Checkley et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Checkley et al., 2008

claim: An estimated 10.9% of global stunting is attributable to diarrhea.
source: An estimated 10.9% of global stunting is attributable to diarrhea (Danaei et al., 2016), and a child with diarrhea is more likely to have a lower HAZ or to die than age-matched controls (Kotloff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Danaei et al., 2016

claim: A child with diarrhea is more likely to have a lower HAZ or to die than age-matched controls.
source: An estimated 10.9% of global stunting is attributable to diarrhea (Danaei et al., 2016), and a child with diarrhea is more likely to have a lower HAZ or to die than age-matched controls (Kotloff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kotloff et al., 2013

claim: There are 1.1 billion episodes of childhood diarrhea that occur globally every year.
source: Given the 1.1 billion episodes of childhood diarrhea that occur globally every year (Collaborators GBDDD, 2018), assessment of children seeking healthcare for diarrhea treatment provides an opportunity to identify those at increased risk for negative outcomes, including stunting and death.
evidence: Supported by citation to Collaborators GBDDD, 2018

claim: Clinical prediction rules (CPRs) are algorithms that aid clinicians in interpreting clinical findings and making clinical decisions.
source: CPRs are algorithms that aid clinicians in interpreting clinical findings and making clinical decisions (Reilly and Evans, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reilly and Evans, 2006

claim: Linear growth faltering captures children whose growth has slowed precipitously and is a precursor of stunting.
source: Linear growth faltering, or falling below standardized height/length growth trajectory projections, captures children whose growth has slowed precipitously and is a precursor of stunting.
evidence: Based on the definition provided in the manuscript

claim: GEMS was a prospective case–control study of acute moderate-to-severe diarrhea (MSD) in children 0–59 months of age.
source: Briefly, GEMS was a prospective case–control study of acute moderate-to-severe diarrhea (MSD) in children 0–59 months of age.
evidence: Description of the GEMS study design

claim: GEMS data were collected in December 2007–March 2011 from seven sites in Africa and Asia.
source: Data were collected in December 2007–March 2011 from seven sites in Africa and Asia, including those in Mali, The Gambia, Kenya, Mozambique, Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan.
evidence: Description of GEMS data collection period and locations

claim: In GEMS, MSD was defined as diarrhea accompanied by one or more of the following: dysentery, dehydration, or hospital admission.
source: MSD was defined as diarrhea accompanied by one or more of the following: dysentery, dehydration, or hospital admission.
evidence: Definition provided in the GEMS study description

claim: In GEMS, diarrhea was defined as new onset (after ≥7 days diarrhea-free) of three or more looser than normal stools in the previous 24 hr lasting 7 days or less.
source: Diarrhea was defined as new onset (after ≥7 days diarrhea-free) of three or more looser than normal stools in the previous 24 hr lasting 7 days or less.
evidence: Definition provided in the GEMS study description

claim: MAL-ED is a longitudinal birth cohort study.
source: We used the Etiology, Risk Factors, and Interactions of Enteric Infections and Malnutrition and the Consequences for Child Health and Development (MAL-ED) study to (1) re-derive the best full model, and (2) externally validate a 2-variable parsimonious version of our GEMS-derived CPR for growth faltering. MAL-ED is a longitudinal birth cohort study, and study details have been described elsewhere (MAL-ED Network Investigators, 2014; Platts-Mills et al., 2014; Platts-Mills et al., 2015; Richard et al., 2014).
evidence: Description of MAL-ED study design with citations

claim: In MAL-ED, healthy children were enrolled within 17 days of birth and followed prospectively through 24 months of age.
source: In brief, healthy children were enrolled within 17 days of birth and followed prospectively through 24 months of age.
evidence: Description of MAL-ED enrollment and follow-up

claim: MAL-ED children were enrolled from October 2009 to March 2012 from eight countries in Asia, Africa, and South America.
source: Children were enrolled from October 2009 to March 2012 from eight countries in Asia, Africa, and South America, including Tanzania, South Africa, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Peru, and Brazil.
evidence: Description of MAL-ED enrollment period and locations

claim: In MAL-ED, diarrhea was defined as maternal report of three or more loose stools in a 24-hr period, or one loose stool with blood.
source: In MAL-ED, diarrhea was defined as maternal report of three or more loose stools in a 24-hr period, or one loose stool with blood.
evidence: Definition provided in the MAL-ED study description

claim: Growth faltering was defined as a decrease in HAZ of ≥0.5 HAZ within 49–91 days of enrollment in GEMS.
source: We defined growth faltering as a decrease in HAZ of ≥0.5 HAZ within 49–91 days of enrollment in GEMS, or within 49–95 days in MAL-ED.
evidence: Definition of the outcome measure in GEMS

claim: Growth faltering was defined as a decrease in HAZ of ≥0.5 HAZ within 49–95 days in MAL-ED.
source: We defined growth faltering as a decrease in HAZ of ≥0.5 HAZ within 49–91 days of enrollment in GEMS, or within 49–95 days in MAL-ED.
evidence: Definition of the outcome measure in MAL-ED

claim: Of 7639 children in GEMS, 1744 (22.8%) experienced severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ).
source: Of 7639 children in GEMS, 1744 (22.8%) experienced severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ).
evidence: Reported in the Abstract and Results sections with data from GEMS analysis

claim: In MAL-ED, 961 (16.9%) episodes experienced severe growth faltering out of 5683 diarrhea episodes from 1322 children.
source: In MAL-ED, we analyzed 5683 diarrhea episodes from 1322 children, of which 961 (16.9%) episodes experienced severe growth faltering.
evidence: Reported in the Abstract with data from MAL-ED analysis

claim: Top predictors of growth faltering in GEMS were: age, HAZ at enrollment, respiratory rate, temperature, and number of people living in the household.
source: Top predictors of growth faltering in GEMS were: age, HAZ at enrollment, respiratory rate, temperature, and number of people living in the household.
evidence: Reported in the Abstract based on random forest variable importance analysis

claim: The maximum area under the curve (AUC) was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.75, 0.75) with 20 predictors in GEMS.
source: The maximum area under the curve (AUC) was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.75, 0.75) with 20 predictors, while 2 predictors yielded an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.71, 0.72).
evidence: Reported in the Abstract based on cross-validated model performance in GEMS

claim: A 2-predictor model yielded an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.71, 0.72) in GEMS.
source: The maximum area under the curve (AUC) was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.75, 0.75) with 20 predictors, while 2 predictors yielded an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.71, 0.72).
evidence: Reported in the Abstract based on cross-validated model performance in GEMS

claim: A 2-variable CPR derived from children 0–23 months in GEMS had an AUC = 0.63 (95% CI: 0.62, 0.65).
source: A 2-variable CPR derived from children 0–23 months in GEMS had an AUC = 0.63 (95% CI: 0.62, 0.65), and AUC = 0.68 (95% CI: 0.63, 0.74) when externally validated in MAL-ED.
evidence: Reported in the Abstract based on model performance in GEMS subset

claim: The 2-variable CPR had an AUC = 0.68 (95% CI: 0.63, 0.74) when externally validated in MAL-ED.
source: A 2-variable CPR derived from children 0–23 months in GEMS had an AUC = 0.63 (95% CI: 0.62, 0.65), and AUC = 0.68 (95% CI: 0.63, 0.74) when externally validated in MAL-ED.
evidence: Reported in the Abstract based on external validation in MAL-ED

claim: 357 (4.7%) children in GEMS experienced very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ).
source: Of the remaining 7639 children, 1744 (22.8%) experienced severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ), and 357 (4.7%) experienced very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ) (Figure 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with data from GEMS analysis

claim: Growth faltering rates differed by country in GEMS, with Mozambique and The Gambia having the highest rates.
source: Growth faltering rates differed by country, with Mozambique and The Gambia having the highest rates of growth faltering (34.5% and 31.9% experienced severe growth faltering, respectively) and Mali having the lowest rate (14.9%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with data from GEMS analysis by country

claim: Mozambique had a growth faltering rate of 34.5% in GEMS.
source: Growth faltering rates differed by country, with Mozambique and The Gambia having the highest rates of growth faltering (34.5% and 31.9% experienced severe growth faltering, respectively) and Mali having the lowest rate (14.9%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with data from GEMS analysis

claim: The Gambia had a growth faltering rate of 31.9% in GEMS.
source: Growth faltering rates differed by country, with Mozambique and The Gambia having the highest rates of growth faltering (34.5% and 31.9% experienced severe growth faltering, respectively) and Mali having the lowest rate (14.9%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with data from GEMS analysis

claim: Mali had the lowest growth faltering rate of 14.9% in GEMS.
source: Growth faltering rates differed by country, with Mozambique and The Gambia having the highest rates of growth faltering (34.5% and 31.9% experienced severe growth faltering, respectively) and Mali having the lowest rate (14.9%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with data from GEMS analysis

claim: Growth faltering rates varied by child's age in GEMS, with a higher proportion of younger children experiencing growth faltering than older children.
source: Growth faltering rates also varied by child's age, with a higher proportion of younger children experiencing growth faltering than older children (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with data from GEMS analysis

claim: In MAL-ED, 161 (2.8%) episodes experienced very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ).
source: Of the remaining 5683 observations from 1322 children, 961 (16.9%) episodes experienced severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ) and 161 (2.8%) episodes experienced very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ, Figure 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with data from MAL-ED analysis

claim: Logistic regression models consistently had higher AUCs than random forest regression models in GEMS.
source: After random forest screening of variables, logistic regression models consistently had higher AUCs than random forest regression models (Figure 2), therefore we only present the easier to interpret logistic regression results moving forward.
evidence: Reported in Results section based on comparison of model types, with reference to Figure 2

claim: The top 10 most predictive variables for severe growth faltering in GEMS included age, HAZ at enrollment, respiratory rate, temperature, number of people living in the household, number of people sleeping in the household, number of days of diarrhea at presentation, number of other households that share same fecal waste disposal facility, whether the child was currently breastfed at time of diarrhea, and the number of children <60 months old living in the household.
source: In Table 1, we show the top 10 most predictive variables ranked from most to least important, for severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ). The top predictive variables for severe growth faltering were: age, HAZ at enrollment, respiratory rate, temperature, number of people living in the household, number of people sleeping in the household, number of days of diarrhea at presentation, number of other households that share same fecal waste disposal facility (e.g., latrine), whether the child was currently breastfed at time of diarrhea, and the number of children <60 months old living in the household.
evidence: Reported in Results section with reference to Table 1, based on random forest variable importance

claim: An AUC of 0.72 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.72) could be obtained with a CPR of 5 variables in GEMS.
source: The maximum AUC attained with the model was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.75, 0.75) with a model of 20 variables, while an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.71, 0.72), 0.72 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.72), and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.72) could be obtained with a CPR of 2, 5, and 10 variables, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: Reported in Results section with reference to Figure 2, based on cross-validated model performance

claim: An AUC of 0.72 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.72) could be obtained with a CPR of 10 variables in GEMS.
source: The maximum AUC attained with the model was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.75, 0.75) with a model of 20 variables, while an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.71, 0.72), 0.72 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.72), and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.72) could be obtained with a CPR of 2, 5, and 10 variables, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: Reported in Results section with reference to Figure 2, based on cross-validated model performance

claim: When limited to children 0–23 months of age in GEMS, AUC decreased to 0.64 (95% CI: 0.64, 0.64) for 10 variables.
source: When limited to children 0–23 months of age, AUC decreased to 0.64 (95% CI: 0.64, 0.64) for 10 variables.
evidence: Reported in Results section based on age-stratified analysis in GEMS

claim: In the full 10-variable model in GEMS, a specificity of 0.47 was achieved at a sensitivity of 0.80.
source: In the full 10-variable model, we achieved a specificity of 0.47 at a sensitivity of 0.80 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The discriminative performance of the full CPR for growth faltering was similar between GEMS and MAL-ED datasets.
source: By utilizing data from two large multicenter clinical studies of pediatric diarrhea, we used a combination of machine learning and conventional regression methods to derive and validate CPRs for linear growth faltering. The discriminative performance of our CPR for growth faltering was remarkably similar between the two datasets (AUC = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.72, 0.72, based on GEMS 0–59 months; 0.68, 95% CI: 0.67, 0.69 based on MAL-ED 0–24 months).
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on comparison of model performance across datasets

claim: The full CPR in GEMS had better discriminative ability than the CPR developed by Brander et al., 2019 (AUC = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.64, 0.69).
source: Our full CPRs were better at identifying growth faltering than (Brander et al., 2019) (AUC = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.64, 0.69), which was not externally validated, and worse than (Hanieh et al., 2019) (AUC = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.80, 0.90), which only used data from a single country.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section comparing performance to prior studies

claim: The full CPR in GEMS had worse discriminative ability than the CPR developed by Hanieh et al., 2019 (AUC = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.80, 0.90).
source: Our full CPRs were better at identifying growth faltering than (Brander et al., 2019) (AUC = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.64, 0.69), which was not externally validated, and worse than (Hanieh et al., 2019) (AUC = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.80, 0.90), which only used data from a single country.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section comparing performance to prior studies

claim: The top predictors of growth faltering identified by random forests were consistent with existing knowledge of the drivers of growth faltering.
source: The top predictors of growth faltering identified by random forests in our analysis were consistent with existing knowledge of the drivers of growth faltering – child demographics, child symptoms, and indicators of household wealth.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on comparison with existing literature

claim: The top 2 variables used in the parsimonious externally validated CPR were age and baseline HAZ.
source: The top 2 variables (used in our parsimonious externally validated CPR) were age and baseline HAZ.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on variable importance analysis

claim: Consideration of additional factors related to nature of disease (etiology, antibiotics) did not improve discriminative ability of the CPR.
source: However, despite the inclusion of markers of disease severity (temperature, respiratory rate, number of days of diarrhea), overall ability to predict growth faltering was moderate, and consideration of additional factors related to nature of disease (etiology, antibiotics) did not improve discriminative ability.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on sensitivity analyses

claim: Treating diarrhea with antibiotics generally did not prevent growth faltering except for Shigella infections.
source: This is consistent with previous analysis in GEMS data that found treating diarrhea with antibiotics generally did not prevent growth faltering (except for Shigella infections, Nasrin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nasrin et al., 2021

claim: The incidence of growth faltering was similar in diarrhea cases and matched controls in GEMS, particularly in the youngest children.
source: Furthermore, the similar incidence of growth faltering in diarrhea cases and matched controls (particularly in the youngest children), as well as the almost identical predictive variables and similar AUCs, suggests that the impact of a single episode of acute diarrhea on growth trajectory may be relatively low.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on comparison of cases and controls

claim: The impact of a single episode of acute diarrhea on growth trajectory may be relatively low.
source: Furthermore, the similar incidence of growth faltering in diarrhea cases and matched controls (particularly in the youngest children), as well as the almost identical predictive variables and similar AUCs, suggests that the impact of a single episode of acute diarrhea on growth trajectory may be relatively low.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of cases and controls in Discussion section

claim: Total days in all diarrheal episodes, days with diarrhea so far this episode, and days since last diarrhea episode were all top 10 predictors of growth faltering in MAL-ED.
source: Indeed, while the design of GEMS does not allow for the exploration of this hypothesis, MAL-ED does. Total days in all diarrheal episodes, days with diarrhea so far this episode, and days since last diarrhea episode were all top 10 predictors of growth faltering in MAL-ED.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on MAL-ED analysis

claim: In GEMS, the average baseline HAZ at enrollment was 0.5 HAZ lower in children who did not experience growth faltering than in children who did.
source: Furthermore in GEMS, the average baseline HAZ at enrollment was 0.5 HAZ lower in children who did not experience growth faltering than in children who did (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), suggesting the possibility that children need to have high enough HAZ in order to have the potential to falter.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5

claim: Children enrolled in Mali had the highest median HAZ at enrollment in GEMS.
source: In contrast, children enrolled in Mali had the highest median HAZ at enrollment, and also had the lowest proportion of children who experienced growth faltering (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Discussion section with reference to Supplementary file 1

claim: Children enrolled in Mali had the lowest proportion of children who experienced growth faltering in GEMS.
source: In contrast, children enrolled in Mali had the highest median HAZ at enrollment, and also had the lowest proportion of children who experienced growth faltering (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Discussion section with reference to Supplementary file 1

claim: The CPR predicting any stunting at follow-up had high accuracy with AUC = 0.90 (95% CI: 0.90, 0.91).
source: In sensitivity analyses, we demonstrated our ability to predict any stunting at follow-up with high accuracy (Table 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: Effective interventions exist for treating acute malnutrition, including exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life.
source: While effective interventions exist for treating acute malnutrition (e.g., exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, inpatient- and community-based management of acute malnutrition using corn-soy blend or ready-to-use therapeutic food; WHO, 2013; Bergeron and Castleman, 2012; Keats et al., 2021), there are few evidence-based guidance on how to reverse the effects of chronic malnutrition once a child is stunted (Bergeron and Castleman, 2012; Leroy et al., 2015; Reinhardt and Fanzo, 2014; Pavlinac et al., 2018; WHO, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to WHO, 2013; Bergeron and Castleman, 2012; Keats et al., 2021

claim: There are few evidence-based guidance on how to reverse the effects of chronic malnutrition once a child is stunted.
source: While effective interventions exist for treating acute malnutrition (e.g., exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, inpatient- and community-based management of acute malnutrition using corn-soy blend or ready-to-use therapeutic food; WHO, 2013; Bergeron and Castleman, 2012; Keats et al., 2021), there are few evidence-based guidance on how to reverse the effects of chronic malnutrition once a child is stunted (Bergeron and Castleman, 2012; Leroy et al., 2015; Reinhardt and Fanzo, 2014; Pavlinac et al., 2018; WHO, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bergeron and Castleman, 2012; Leroy et al., 2015; Reinhardt and Fanzo, 2014; Pavlinac et al., 2018; WHO, 2015

claim: Approximately one in five children experience severe growth faltering subsequent to acute diarrhea.
source: We found that approximately one in five children experience severe growth faltering subsequent to acute diarrhea, that is, an additional ≥0.5 decrease in HAZ in the 2–3 months after acute diarrhea.
evidence: Reported in Discussion section based on GEMS data analysis

claim: Random forests are an ensemble learning method whereby multiple decision trees are built on bootstrapped samples of the data.
source: Random forests are an ensemble learning method whereby multiple decision trees (1000 throughout this analysis) are built on bootstrapped samples of the data with only a random sample of potential predictors considered at each split, thereby decorrelating the trees and reducing variability (James et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to James et al., 2013

claim: 1000 decision trees were used in the random forest analysis throughout this study.
source: Random forests are an ensemble learning method whereby multiple decision trees (1000 throughout this analysis) are built on bootstrapped samples of the data with only a random sample of potential predictors considered at each split, thereby decorrelating the trees and reducing variability (James et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Methods section describing the random forest approach

claim: Generalizable performance was assessed using fivefold repeated cross-validation.
source: Generalizable performance was assessed using fivefold repeated cross-validation.
evidence: Stated in the Methods section describing model validation approach

claim: When MUAC was considered as a potential predictor instead of HAZ, AUC decreased to 0.70 (95% CI: 0.70, 0.70).
source: When MUAC was considered as a potential predictor (instead of HAZ), MUAC replaced HAZ as a top predictor, all other top 10 predictors remained the same, and AUC decreased (down to 0.70, 95% CI: 0.70, 0.70).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: When both HAZ and MUAC were considered as potential predictors, AUC remained unchanged compared to the main model that considered only HAZ (0.72, 95% CI: 0.72, 0.73).
source: When both HAZ and MUAC were considered as potential predictors, both were top predictors, but AUC remained unchanged compared to the main model that considered only HAZ (0.72, 95% CI: 0.72, 0.73).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: The predictors of very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ) were similar to the predictors of severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ).
source: The predictors of very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ) were similar to the predictors of severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ), though predictive ability was better (AUC 0.80 [95% CI: 0.79, 0.80] for ≥1.0 vs. 0.72 [95% CI: 0.71, 0.73] for ≥0.5).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: Predictive ability for very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ) was better than for severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ), with AUC 0.80 vs. 0.72.
source: The predictors of very severe growth faltering (≥1.0 decrease in HAZ) were similar to the predictors of severe growth faltering (≥0.5 decrease in HAZ), though predictive ability was better (AUC 0.80 [95% CI: 0.79, 0.80] for ≥1.0 vs. 0.72 [95% CI: 0.71, 0.73] for ≥0.5).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: Accounting for seasonality did not meaningfully improve the CPR.
source: Accounting for seasonality did not meaningfully improve the CPR, and antibiotic use and diarrhea etiology were consistently not ranked as top predictors of growth faltering (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: Antibiotic use and diarrhea etiology were consistently not ranked as top predictors of growth faltering.
source: Accounting for seasonality did not meaningfully improve the CPR, and antibiotic use and diarrhea etiology were consistently not ranked as top predictors of growth faltering (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: When data were limited to only those children not already stunted at initial presentation, top predictors and AUC of growth faltering were similar (0.71, 95% CI: 0.70, 0.72).
source: When data were limited to only those children not already stunted at initially presentation, top predictors and AUC of growth faltering were similar (0.71, 95% CI: 0.70, 0.72).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on sensitivity analysis

claim: Top predictors of growth faltering were similar in non-diarrhea controls compared to cases in GEMS.
source: Top predictors of growth faltering were similar in non-diarrhea controls compared to cases in GEMS (Table 1), but predictive ability was higher (AUC 0.79 [95% CI: 0.78, 0.79] in controls vs. 0.72 [95% CI: 0.72, 0.72] in cases).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on analysis of controls

claim: Predictive ability for growth faltering was higher in non-diarrhea controls than in cases in GEMS (AUC 0.79 vs. 0.72).
source: Top predictors of growth faltering were similar in non-diarrhea controls compared to cases in GEMS (Table 1), but predictive ability was higher (AUC 0.79 [95% CI: 0.78, 0.79] in controls vs. 0.72 [95% CI: 0.72, 0.72] in cases).
evidence: Reported in Results section based on analysis of controls

claim: The maximum AUC attained with the model in controls was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.79, 0.80) with a model of 15 variables.
source: The maximum AUC attained with the model was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.79, 0.80) with a model of 15 variables, while an AUC of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.78, 0.79) and 0.79 (95% CI: 0.79, 0.79) could be obtained with a CPR of 5 and 10 variables, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Reported in Results section for controls analysis with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: CPRs of higher age strata had higher AUCs (0.76 in 24–59 months vs. 0.60 in 0–11 months in GEMS).
source: CPRs of higher age strata had higher AUCs (0.76 [95% CI: 0.75, 0.77] in 24–59 months in GEMS vs. 0.60 [95% CI: 0.59, 0.60] in 0–11 months in GEMS).
